## Executive summary

A price increase can offset lost sales, but the allowable volume loss depends
on the business's starting margin. This report calculates the maximum volume
loss that leaves total contribution profit unchanged under a simplified,
constant-unit-cost model. It applies to businesses at any margin; lower-margin
businesses have a larger break-even volume-loss threshold for the same price
increase.

The calculation is a break-even threshold, not a forecast of how customers
will respond. Replace the example scenarios with company-specific margins and
price changes before drawing business conclusions.

## The break-even calculation

Let the original unit price be \(P\), the contribution margin be \(m\), and
the price increase be \(r\), where both \(m\) and \(r\) are expressed as
decimals. Original unit cost is \(P(1-m)\). After the price increase, unit
contribution is:

\[
P(1+r) - P(1-m) = P(m+r).
\]

If \(q\) is the fraction of original volume retained, equal total contribution
profit requires \(qP(m+r) = Pm\). Therefore:

\[
\text{maximum volume loss} = 1-q = \frac{r}{m+r}.
\]

For example, a 10% price increase gives a break-even volume loss of
\(0.10/(0.05+0.10) \approx 66.7\%\) at a 5% margin, and
\(0.10/(0.40+0.10) = 20\%\) at a 40% margin.

## Scenarios

Edit the vectors below to model different margins and price increases.
Margins must be between 0% and 100%; price increases must be positive.

```{r}
max_volume_loss <- function(margin, price_raise) {
  if (any(!is.finite(margin)) || any(margin < 0 | margin >= 1)) {
    stop("Margins must be finite values from 0 (inclusive) to 1 (exclusive).")
  }
  if (any(!is.finite(price_raise)) || any(price_raise <= 0)) {
    stop("Price increases must be finite, positive values.")
  }

  price_raise / (margin + price_raise)
}

scenarios <- data.frame(
  company = c("Low-margin example", "Higher-margin example"),
  margin = c(0.05, 0.40),
  price_raise = c(0.10, 0.10)
)

scenarios$max_volume_loss <- max_volume_loss(
  scenarios$margin,
  scenarios$price_raise
)
scenarios$volume_retained <- 1 - scenarios$max_volume_loss

report_table <- data.frame(
  Company = scenarios$company,
  `Starting margin` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * scenarios$margin),
  `Price increase` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * scenarios$price_raise),
  `Maximum volume loss` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * scenarios$max_volume_loss),
  `Volume retained at break-even` =
    sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * scenarios$volume_retained),
  check.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(report_table, caption = "Illustrative break-even scenarios")
```

## Interpreting the results

At the break-even threshold, the higher contribution per remaining sale exactly
offsets the contribution lost from lower volume. A volume loss below the
threshold increases total contribution profit in this model; a loss above it
reduces total contribution profit.

The threshold alone does not show whether a price increase is achievable.
Estimate customer-level price sensitivity, consider competitor and contract
effects, and check whether costs or customer mix change with volume.
